caption:
The International Court of Justice has officially ruled that Myanmar committed genocide.

This is the first time in history a country has been found guilty of this specific crime.

Beyond the immediate impact for Rohingya victims, the court’s decision provides a new legal framework. It sets a precedent for how judges assess the intent behind mass violence.

Legal experts are already looking at how this roadmap might apply to other ongoing conflicts. It is a rare moment of accountability in international law.

story.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
story.summary: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused
